title: The participle as an adjective
description: Describe a person by what they have done, or what is being done to them.
grammarNote: A participle can work as an adjective: una casa abandonada, an abandoned house.

explanation.summary: The participle is not only for the passive. It can describe a thing or a person on its own, and then it behaves like an adjective, including the agreement.

sections.heading: Describing with the participle
sections.body: A participle after the noun describes it: un coche aparcado, a parked car; una mujer cansada, a tired woman. It agrees with the noun like any other adjective: un coche aparcado, but una coche aparcada. And the difference from an adjective is that the participle keeps the action inside it: cansado means tired because of the doing.

sections.heading: How it differs from estar
sections.body: Estar plus a participle says the action is happening now: está quemando, it is burning. The participle on its own says the state it left behind: la cocina está sucia, the kitchen is dirty, but la cocina está ensuciada, the kitchen has been made dirty, by somebody. Spanish makes that difference, and English mostly does not.

examples.note: The participle goes after the noun.

items.note: The participle of abandonar. It agrees: abandonada.
The participle of cansar. It agrees: cansada.
